subject: Future Tech
title: How the Sun Does It
description: A micro-lesson that makes How the Sun Does It usable.

hook.text: The sun's core is 15 million degrees and crushes atoms with gravity 250 billion times Earth's.

buildup.text: Hydrogen nuclei normally repel each other. The sun's massive gravity overcomes this repulsion and forces them together.

discovery.text: When two hydrogen nuclei fuse into helium, a tiny bit of mass converts to enormous energy, following E = mc².

twist.text: On Earth, we can't replicate the sun's gravity. So we must heat plasma to 100 million degrees—hotter than the sun.

climax.text: What the sun does with size the Earth must do with temperature. It's the same physics, just a different approach.

punchline.text: We can't build a sun. But we can out-heat one.

quiz.question: Why must Earth-based fusion be hotter than the sun?
options: We can't replicate the sun's gravitational pressure
Earth's atmosphere absorbs too much heat
